articles.title: Bill Gates' $3.9 million-a-week superyacht has one rule that forces guests off for six hours
articles.standfirst: A dream superyacht, amenities beyond imagination and one unusual feature few would expect to find on a vessel of this caliber.
articles.summary: A dream superyacht, amenities beyond imagination and one unusual feature few would expect to find on a vessel of this caliber.
articles.body:
Imagining a vacation aboard Breakthrough means picturing an experience where seemingly nothing is missing. The 118.8-meter superyacht features ocean-view suites, balconies that extend over the water, a gym, sauna, private cinema and even an underwater lounge with windows offering views of marine life. Everything is designed for an extraordinary luxury getaway, with charter rates reaching $3.9 million per week .

But Breakthrough also has a rather unusual backstory. Its construction was originally commissioned by Bill Gates, Microsoft's co-founder, although he never actually stepped aboard once the superyacht was completed . Some time later, the vessel was acquired by Canadian billionaire Patrick Dovigi, an environmental services entrepreneur and former professional hockey goaltender.

However, beyond the man who commissioned its construction and the impressive amenities it offers, Breakthrough has one particular feature its guests need to keep in mind: whenever it's time to replenish the liquid hydrogen used by one of its power systems, everyone must leave the yacht for approximately six hours. It's a mandatory break that means leaving behind the suites, terraces and all those luxuries to continue the vacation on land.

Why can't anyone stay aboard during refueling?

It all comes down to the fuel used by one of the yacht's power systems. Breakthrough stores approximately four metric tons of liquid hydrogen in a cryogenic tank, which keeps it at a temperature close to -423 degrees Fahrenheit . This fuel requires very specific handling conditions because it can be highly flammable when it comes into contact with oxygen.

That's why refueling isn't an operation that can take place while guests continue enjoying the yacht's facilities. Before the process begins, a safety perimeter is established around the superyacht, and everyone must disembark. From that point on, the operation is handled by specialized personnel.

The process starts with purging the pipes with nitrogen and gradually cooling down the system. Only then does the fuel transfer begin. During this operation, excess gaseous hydrogen is released through a venting structure located on the mast, known as the needle.

So, no matter how much Breakthrough has to offer for an extraordinary vacation, there's one thing even its millions of dollars can't change: when it's time to refuel with hydrogen, everyone has to get off the yacht.
